requirements.requirement: node2 placed on VLAN 10 over the shared trunk link
requirements.summary: nmcli created vlan10 sub-interface (10.10.10.2/24) on enp8s0 trunk; confirmed present pre- and post-reboot.

requirements.requirement: node3 placed on VLAN 20 over the shared trunk link
requirements.summary: nmcli created vlan20 sub-interface (10.10.20.2/24) on enp8s0 trunk; confirmed present pre- and post-reboot.

requirements.requirement: node1 routes between the VLANs so node2 and node3 can reach each other
requirements.summary: VyOS eth1.10 (10.10.10.1/24) and eth1.20 (10.10.20.1/24) configured with ip_forward=1; node2<->node3 pings succeed with TTL=63, confirming one router hop through node1, both before and after full-cluster reboot cycle.

requirements.requirement: Implementation done via Ansible from the designated control node (node4)
requirements.summary: A playbook (/root/vlan-segmentation.yml) and inventory were authored on node4 and executed with ansible-playbook against node1/node2/node3, applying all VLAN and routing configuration.

requirements.requirement: Playbook converges correctly and is idempotent on repeat runs
requirements.summary: Final playbook run after fixes reports changed=0 across all managed hosts, confirming full convergence with no residual drift.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task were satisfied: node2 was placed on VLAN 10 and node3 on VLAN 20 over their shared trunk with node1 (VyOS), which was configured with matching eth1.10/eth1.20 sub-interfaces and IP forwarding to route between them. Ansible was used from the designated control node (node4) to apply all configuration, and the final playbook run is idempotent (changed=0). The executor additionally ran the full node-restart evidence protocol on all four nodes, each showing a healthy pre-restart baseline, an acknowledged reboot, a changed boot identity, and recovered VLAN/routing state plus a final idempotent Ansible re-run and successful cross-VLAN ping — directly demonstrating the disruption-and-recovery transition required for this class of evidence. Hygiene is slightly reduced by one unnecessary troubleshooting mutation on node1 (an out-of-scope eth1.30 vif) that was reverted, and by an unexplained but reboot-related NetworkManager-wait-online failed-service state appearing on node2/node3 after the restart cycle.
limitations: The NetworkManager-wait-online.service failure appearing on node2/node3 post-reboot was not investigated by the executor or explained in the trace; it does not appear to affect functional VLAN/routing state based on the successful post-reboot pings, but its root cause is unconfirmed.

Evidence for the restart protocol relies on command outputs interleaved with executor narration rather than the fixed lifecycle snapshot phases matching 1:1 to each individual reboot, though the fixed before/after-executor snapshots corroborate the boot-id transitions for all four nodes.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands were legitimate iteration toward the working playbook (creating/deleting/recreating VLAN interfaces and VyOS vif config while debugging), and residue from these was cleaned up before the final working state (cmd-b867994093fb48a0, cmd-5e498fe2ba5d4c54, cmd-7fb4589724964e25 deleted the intermediate vlan10/vlan20/eth1.vif configs). However, cmd-113108dfef78498f applied an out-of-scope VyOS interface (eth1.30/10.10.30.1/24) purely as a troubleshooting experiment to diagnose sudo/config-session behavior on node1; this was unrelated to the vlan10/vlan20 task scope, though it was subsequently reverted in cmd-b16ccdc4185d482a leaving no final residue. Post-executor lifecycle diff shows NetworkManager-wait-online.service in a failed state on node2 and node3 after reboot, which is residual disruption from the reboot protocol rather than the VLAN task itself, and was not investigated or remediated by the executor. No unsafe exposure, credential leakage in final state, or damaged package state was observed.
